problem: Semantic SLAM cannot use the meaning of scene text, and text-based SLAM only exploits the planar geometry of text rather than what it says. So SLAM maps cannot answer natural-language queries or guide a user to a place.
motivation: Humans read signs (shop names, warnings) to decide where to go, and robots should be able to do the same. OCR output is noisy (misrecognition, false detections, repeated observations), so a naive text map is unreliable. LLMs can repair noisy text, judge what a landmark is, and map free-form user requests to map locations.
key_idea: Add scene-text recognition on top of ORB-SLAM2 and use ChatGPT for text clustering, landmark judgement and natural-language navigation queries over a text-landmark map, with similarity classification and a long-short-term memory to filter OCR errors.
insight: OCR noise can be handled with cheap non-learned filters (Levenshtein similarity grouping plus a frequency-based memory with forgetting) before the LLM is used to pick the correct spelling. A few-shot 'pre-train' prompt is enough to make ChatGPT return machine-parsable outputs without any training. Evidence is qualitative only (figures and one table), with no ablations or quantitative metrics.
method: Scene text recognition: DBNet detection plus CRNN recognition (OpenCV) on RGB frames; detections whose boxes fall outside an image-position threshold are discarded.
Similarity classification: normalized Levenshtein similarity Sim(A,B)=1-D/max(m,n) groups misspelled variants of the same text into homologous classes; low-similarity strings are discarded.

Long-short-term memory: each class gets a memory score that grows with observations and decays every frame (forgetting); classes above a threshold move to long-term memory, which removes rare mis-detections.
ChatGPT text cluster: a few-shot prompt makes ChatGPT pick the most reasonable name from each class of misspelled variants, in English and Chinese.
Landmark judgement: ChatGPT is prompted to output [[1]] or [[0]] for whether a text is a shop name; texts judged 0 are removed from the map.

Position calculation and clustering: each text's pixel position (mean of the box corners) is back-projected with depth and the camera pose into world coordinates. Per class, N iterations of averaging and dropping the 20% farthest points remove outliers.
Navigation: the list of landmark names and coordinates is given to ChatGPT with a query in any language. ChatGPT returns the chosen landmark and SLAM returns its coordinates.

setting.backbone: ChatGPT (frozen, prompted) + DBNet/CRNN scene text recognition + ORB-SLAM2
setting.training_data: none (training-free; few-shot prompts for ChatGPT, pretrained OCR)
setting.observation: RGB-D (Intel RealSense D435i) with camera pose from ORB-SLAM2
setting.action_space: none; outputs a target landmark coordinate for a downstream navigation algorithm

numbers_note: No quantitative metrics; results are qualitative figures and a landmark-judgement table (Table I) with binary per-landmark outputs.
results: In a mock-mall test on a Roban humanoid, the system correctly judged shop names (KFC, Pizza Hut, ALIENWARE, HUAWEI, GUCCI) as landmarks. It rejected warning slogans and facilities such as DANGER and washroom, but also wrongly rejected 'Donotbeat' style slogans as expected while missing none of the shops. It cleaned noisy OCR text and answered English, Chinese and Japanese queries with the correct landmark. No baselines or numeric metrics were reported.
limitations: Evaluation is purely qualitative in a small mock mall, with no metrics, baselines or ablations.
Relies on prompt-engineered ChatGPT (an external API) and OCR that still makes mistakes; there is no closed-loop navigation, only a target coordinate output.
Language information is not used to improve SLAM accuracy or efficiency.
